It was developed to address the challenge of visualizing vector fields where the dominant free stream flow obscures interesting features [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the technique was developed to address the challenge of visualizing vector fields where dominant free stream flow obscures interesting features. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'If the magnitude of the perturbation velocity vector is mapped to opacity, the bulk of irrelevant free stream flow is invisible.' It further explains that subtracting the free stream velocity yields the perturbation velocity, and that negative values (flow slower than free stream) are mapped to be opaque and visible, while the rest is made invisible. This directly supports the claim that the method addresses the obscuring effect of the free stream flow.

Typically, a magnitude of zero (matching the free stream) results in zero opacity, making the free stream invisible, while non-zero magnitudes result in higher opacity [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that subtracting the free stream velocity yields the perturbation velocity. It further states that 'If the magnitude of the perturbation velocity vector is mapped to opacity, the bulk of irrelevant free stream flow is invisible.' In the free stream, the local velocity equals the free stream velocity, so the perturbation velocity is zero. Mapping this zero magnitude to opacity results in invisibility (zero opacity). Conversely, regions with non-zero perturbation (disturbed flow) have non-zero magnitudes, which are mapped to visible opacity. Thus, the claim is fully supported by the text.
supported

*   **When to use:** When the primary interest is in flow structures caused by obstacles or interactions, rather than the absolute speed of the fluid [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the technique is used when the primary interest is in flow structures caused by obstacles or interactions, rather than absolute speed. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports this by stating that mapping the magnitude of the perturbation velocity (which represents the deviation from free stream flow, i.e., interactions/obstacles) to opacity makes the 'bulk of irrelevant free stream flow invisible.' This implies the focus is on the perturbations (structures caused by obstacles) rather than the free stream (absolute speed). The evidence details how perturbation velocity is calculated (local minus free stream) and visualized to highlight these specific flow features.
